431.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away, as gold is dissolved by borax.”
431.explanation: In the Dakhanee Oankaar Guru Nanak names lust (kaam) and anger (krodh), two of the five thieves, as forces that quietly wear a person down from within, as borax melts gold.
431.tie_back: The Kural says prosperity has dignity only when it is free of lust, anger and arrogance; Guru Nanak shows the same faults eating away at the person who harbours them.
431.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee (Dakhanee Oankaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
431._accuracy_note: A strong fit on two of the Kural's three faults (lust and anger); arrogance is not named in this line, and the Guru speaks of spiritual ruin rather than a ruler's honour.

432.quote_or_event: “Ego is a chronic disease, but it contains its own cure as well.”
432.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Angad calls haumai (ego) a long-lasting disease of the self, yet one that can be cured through the Guru's grace and the Shabad.
432.tie_back: The Kural lists misplaced pride among the faults that harm a ruler; Guru Angad treats that same self-swelling as a chronic sickness that must be treated, not indulged.
432.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
432._accuracy_note: Matches only the pride element of the Kural's triad; avarice and unseemly delight are not addressed, and the Gurbani point is spiritual rather than political.

433.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, I am the worst of all. Everyone else is good.”
433.explanation: Bhagat Kabir models a humility that looks hard at one's own failings and refuses to rank oneself above anyone else.
433.tie_back: The Kural praises those who see a millet-sized fault in themselves as large as a palmyra; Kabir's self-judgement magnifies his own faults in the same spirit.
433.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1364, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
433._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on magnifying one's own faults; Kabir's line is about humility before God and others, without the Kural's explicit dread of public disgrace.

434.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism.”
434.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the real robbers are not outside but within: the five vices that plunder the treasure of the Naam.
434.tie_back: The Kural says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin and must be guarded against; Sikh teaching likewise locates the true enemy in the five thieves inside the self.
434.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
434._accuracy_note: A close parallel: both treat inner faults as the real enemy; the Kural frames this as political prudence, Gurbani as the struggle against haumai and the five vices.

435.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukh has forgotten the Naam. He is like straw, burning in the forest fire.”
435.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the person who lives by his own will and forgets the divine Name to dry straw consumed by a forest fire.
435.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who does not guard against faults beforehand perishes like a heap of straw before fire; Guru Nanak uses the same image of straw in fire for the unguarded, self-willed life.
435.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 63, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
435._accuracy_note: The straw-in-fire image matches closely, but Gurbani's cause of ruin is forgetting the Naam rather than failing to foresee faults, so the parallel is partial.

436.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
436.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the wise to stop recording others' wrongs and to look first into their own conduct.
436.tie_back: The Kural asks the ruler to remove his own faults first and only then examine others'; Farid gives exactly this order of self-scrutiny before judging anyone else.
436.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
436._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on looking at one's own faults before others'; Farid advises refraining from judging others at all, while the Kural permits judging once one's own faults are gone.

437.quote_or_event: “The bee stores up loads of honey; then someone comes and takes the honey, and throws dust in its mouth.” … “He takes the wealth of Maya, and buries it in the ground.” … “His wealth remains buried in the ground, while his body turns to dust.”
437.explanation: Bhagat Namdev describes the hoarder who toils for wealth and buries it, only to leave it in the ground at death, like the bee whose stored honey is taken by another.
437.tie_back: The Kural says the miser's wealth, never put to its proper use, perishes without benefit; Namdev's buried treasure and robbed honey make the same point.
437.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1252, Raag Saarang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
437._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on hoarded wealth coming to nothing; Namdev's remedy is the Saadh Sangat and remembrance of God rather than the Kural's giving and enjoyment, though Sikh teaching also enjoins vand chhakna (sharing).

438.quote_or_event: “O mortal, why have you attached yourself to greed, and lost the jewel of life?”
438.explanation: Bhagat Kabir warns that clinging greed (lobh) squanders the priceless human birth.
438.tie_back: The Kural sets the grasping, clinging heart of avarice apart as a fault beyond all others; Kabir likewise treats attachment to greed as the loss of life's single jewel.
438.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
438._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on greed as a clinging attachment with grave cost; Kabir does not rank greed above every other fault as the Kural does.

439.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good — goodness shall not draw near him.”
439.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan teaches that self-praise is itself a mark of haumai, and that the person who proclaims his own goodness drives goodness away.
439.tie_back: The Kural forbids admiring oneself at any time; Guru Arjan states that self-congratulation empties a person of the very virtue he claims.
439.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
439._accuracy_note: A close match on the first half of the Kural (no self-admiration); the second half, not desiring fruitless deeds, is not covered by this line.

440.quote_or_event: “They are close to the Lord, but they do not reveal their secret to anyone.”
440.explanation: Sheikh Farid describes true devotees who keep their inner love for God private rather than displaying it.
440.tie_back: The Kural advises enjoying what one loves without others knowing one's desires; Farid praises a similar reticence about one's deepest longing, though for spiritual rather than strategic reasons.
440.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
440._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Kural's point is political secrecy to thwart enemies' schemes, which has no real Sikh counterpart; Farid's line shares only the idea of keeping one's inner love hidden.
